sec.title: Purpose
sec.p: Corneal thickness is a key measurement in ophthalmology, playing a significant role in diagnosing and monitoring conditions such as keratoconus, corneal dystrophies, and glaucoma, as well as in the preoperative evaluation for refractive surgery and keratoplasty. This study aimed to compare corneal thickness measurements obtained using a Scheimpflug-based imaging system with a new optical coherence tomographer.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This prospective study enrolled Polish patients with healthy eyes. Measurements were performed using the two devices, the Oculus Pentacam and Optopol Revo FC, in a random sequence. The agreement between the devices was evaluated using correlation coefficients, Bland-Altman analysis, and a paired t-test.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 74 patients were examined. The central corneal thickness measured by Pentacam was 545.52 ± 30.16 μm, while 539.36 ± 30.16 μm for Revo FC (difference 5.52 μm; 95% CI: 4.42 to 6.61; p < 0.01). The thinnest corneal location measured by Pentacam was 540.93 ± 30.20 μm, while 531.04 ± 30.24 μm for Revo FC (difference 9.27 μm; 95% CI: 7.29 to 10.76; p< 0.01). However, the strong intraclass correlation coefficients (0.99 for central and 0.98 for minimum corneal thickness) indicate a high level of agreement between the two imaging systems.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study demonstrated that corneal thickness measurements with Pentacam were greater than with Revo FC OCT. Although highly correlated, the results cannot be considered interchangeable as the mean differences exceeded clinically acceptable limits.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Corneal thickness is a key measurement in ophthalmology that enables continuous monitoring and diagnosis of patients affected by specific ophthalmic conditions, such as keratoconus, corneal dystrophies, contact lens use, and glaucoma, as well as evaluating patients for upcoming interventions, including refractive surgery and keratoplasty [1]. In refractive surgery, accurate corneal thickness measurements allow precise planning of the operation and estimation of how much corneal tissue can be safely removed to achieve the desired refractive outcomes [2]. This assessment is essential for qualifying patients for refractive surgery, ensuring the safety of the procedure [3]. Such measurements enable us to exclude contraindicated corneal conditions and estimate the probability of postoperative complications, such as iatrogenic corneal ectasia [4]. In all corneal refractive surgery methods including laser-assisted in-situ keratomileusis, photorefractive keratectomy and small incision lenticule extraction, maintaining a residual stromal bed of 250 μm is generally considered sufficient to significantly reduce the risk of iatrogenic keratectasia [5, 6].

Corneal thickness is also used to detect keratoconus, a condition characterized by cone-like steepening of the cornea and irregular stromal thinning [7]. Pachymetric maps describing changes from the thinnest point to the periphery provide valuable insight into corneal biomechanics and disease progression [8]. These measurements are particularly crucial for evaluating pathologies, such as keratoconus, as they reveal structural alterations in the cornea [8]. Current optical coherence tomography (OCT) systems allow detailed pachymetric and keratometric analysis of both stromal and epithelial layers [9]. In keratoconus, epithelial thinning over the cone surrounded by a ring of thickened epithelium has been described, while pellucid marginal degeneration presents with arcuate thinning in the inferior cornea [10].

Although some previous studies have evaluated corneal thickness measurements with the Revo OCT system (OPTOPOL Technology, Zawiercie, Poland; software version 11.5) [11, 12], only one has evaluated the technically improved version of the device, the Revo FC [13]. This new version offers faster scan acquisition, improved segmentation algorithms, and integrated fundus imaging, which enhance image quality and measurement reliability. Therefore, this study aimed to compare corneal thickness measurements obtained using the Pentacam Scheimpflug-based imaging system and the new Revo FC OCT system.

sec.title: Study setting and population
sec.p: This prospective study enrolled subjects with healthy eyes at the Hygeia Clinic, Gdańsk, Poland and ArtLife Ophthalmological Center, Gdańsk, Poland, between November 2023 and May 2024. This study was approved by the local research ethics board (Komisja Bioetyczna przy Izbie Lekarskiej w Gdańsku) and adhered to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki for the use of human participants in biomedical research. All subjects provided written informed consent after being informed of the purpose of this study. The exclusion criteria were any ocular disease (including cataract), corrected distance visual acuity worse than 20/25, and previous ocular surgery or trauma. Before enrollment, all eyes underwent a complete ophthalmological examination, including subjective refraction, non-contact tonometry, slit-lamp examination and ophthalmoscopy. Myopia was defined as a spherical equivalent < − 0.5 D, and hyperopia was defined as a spherical equivalent ≥ 2.0 D [14].

sec.title: Instruments
sec.p: The Pentacam (OCULUS Optikgeräte GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany) is a rotational Scheimpflug camera that uses a 475 nm blue light source to capture three-dimensional, non-contact images of the anterior segment. It performs a single scan by acquiring 25 cross-sectional images at angles ranging from 0° to 180°, gathering 25,000 data points in approximately 1–2 s.

In contrast, the Revo FC is an spectral domain-OCT device that employs an 830 nm superluminescent laser diode as its light source. This standard OCT imaging system, can generate corneal tomography images using a dedicated module available in software version 9.0 and newer. In this mode, it captures 16 cross-sectional scans of the cornea over an 8 mm diameter in under 1 s. The Revo FC OCT represents a technically enhanced version of the earlier Revo models. Compared to previous models (Revo 60/80), the Revo FC operates at a higher scan speed of up to 130,000 A-scans per second, reducing motion artifacts and improving measurement repeatability. It also features an integrated 12.3-megapixel non-mydriatic fundus camera, allowing precise scan centration and simultaneous evaluation of the posterior segment. In addition to central corneal thickness (CCT) measurements, the Revo FC OCT allows epithelial thickness mapping. Although the device performance may evolve with subsequent technical upgrades, previous studies have evaluated the repeatability and reproducibility of corneal thickness measurements with the Revo FC OCT [12, 13]. Thus, these parameters have not been evaluated in the current study.

Both devices were calibrated according to the manufacturer’s guidelines before each measurement session to minimize inter-device variability. The measurements were performed with the two systems in random order. Only the right eye was analyzed to avoid inter-eye correlation, which could bias statistical comparisons [15]. All scans were conducted between 9:00 and 18:00. Two skilled operators performed three scans each with the Revo FC OCT in random order, obtaining three measurements per eye.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were performed using Prism (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA) and MedCalc statistical software (version 21; Medcalc Software, Ostend, Belgium), with a p value less than < 0.05 considered statistically significant. As the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test indicated that all parameters were normally distributed, they are presented as means ± standard deviations (SD) and were compared between systems using correlation coefficients, the Bland–Altman method, and paired t-tests [15].

sec.title: Results
sec.p: This study included 74 patients (29 men and 45 women) with a mean age of 36.50 ± 10.54 years. Across the examined eyes, the mean flat keratometry value was 42.89 ± 1.42, and the mean steep keratometry value was 44.06 ± 1.53. The mean keratometric astigmatism was 1.17 ± 0.95 D. The mean spherical equivalent refraction was − 1.40 ± 3.21 with 47 (58.11%) patients being myopic, and 11 (14.86%) being hyperopic.

The mean CCT was 545.52 ± 30.16 μm with the Pentacam system and 539.36 ± 30.16 μm with the Revo FC OCT (Table 1). The mean difference between the systems was 5.52 ± 4.70 μm (95% confidence interval [CI]: 4.42 to 6.61; p < 0.01). The CCT measurements of the two systems had a correlation coefficient of 0.99 (limits of agreement: −3.70 to 14.74 μm). The Bland–Altman plot for CCT is shown in Fig. 1.

sec.p: The thinnest corneal thickness was 540.93 ± 30.20 μm with the Pentacam system and 531.04 ± 30.24 μm with the Revo FC OCT. The mean difference between systems was 9.27 μm (95% CI: 7.29 to 10.76; p < 0.01). The thinnest corneal thickness measurements of the two systems had a correlation coefficient of 0,98 (limits of agreement: -3.17 to 21.72). The Bland-Altman plot for the central corneal thickness is shown in Fig. 1, while the plot for thinnest corneal thickness is shown in Fig. 2.

sec.p: The mean epithelial thickness measured with the Revo FC OCT was 55.18 ± 2.84 μm, with a median of 55 μm. The mean epithelial thickness at the thinnest point was 54.20 ± 2.87 μm. Epithelial thickness could not be evaluated using the Pentacam system.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study has demonstrated minor differences in both central and minimum corneal thickness measurements between a Pentacam Scheimpflug camera and the Revo FC OCT. The difference was slightly greater for minimum corneal thickness (9.27 ± 6.35 μm) than for CCT (5.52 ± 4.70). However, the high correlation coefficients for CCT (0.99) and minimum corneal thickness (0.98) indicated strong agreement between the systems. In most cases, mean differences of 5–9 μm are unlikely to influence routine clinical decisions. However, when assessing eligibility for refractive surgery, this discrepancy between systems should be considered when assessing the residual stromal bed in laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis. In addition, these differences in corneal thickness must be taken into account when evaluating keratoconus progression. Using the same system for longitudinal monitoring of keratoconus progression with stromal measurements and epithelial thickness maps may help ensure consistency and accurate clinical interpretation [16, 17].

Analysis of corneal thickness measurements across various studies reveals noticeable differences depending on the imaging technique used (Table 2). Among the examined studies, the largest difference was observed by Milla et al., who reported a difference of 22.4 ± 10.4 μm between Sirius (Scheimpflug imaging) and Visante (time-domain OCT) systems [26]. Similarly, Ishibazawa et al. reported a significant difference of -22.0 ± 9.0 μm between the Pentacam (Scheimpflug imaging) and RTVue-100 (spectral domain OCT) systems [25]. In contrast, studies such as Randleman et al. and Huang et al. found relatively small discrepancies between the Pentacam (Scheimpflug imaging) and RTVue-100 (spectral domain OCT) systems of 2.3 ± 9.9 μm [21] and 6.0 ± 4.8 μm [22], respectively, with Pentacam yielding higher values. Other studies not included in Table 2 have also shown that systems based on Scheimpflug imaging provide higher values than those based on OCT systems. One study comparing the reproducibility and repeatability of corneal topography between the Galilei G6 (Scheimpflug imaging), Casia 2 (OCT), and Revo NX (OCT) demonstrated differences in CCT measurements (569.13 ± 37.58 μm, 545.00 ± 36.15 μm, and 537.39 ± 35.92 μm, respectively) [12]. Another study examining CCT measurements reported a similar difference between Pentacam (Scheimpflug imaging) and Revo (OCT) systems (550.74 ± 31.55 μm vs. 535.54 ± 32.45 μm) [11]. While Maloca et al. reported little difference between the measurement methods [20], the large standard deviation they observed may indicate variability in measurements obtained with the same system within the study group, possibly due to factors such as patient age, as their study included subjects aged 20–86 years [20]. Differences across studies may also be due to differences in measurement technologies and sample sizes, as well as subject heterogeneity. However, most found measurements obtained with both technologies to be comparable, though dependent on the clinical context, since crucial decisions often rely on them [18].

sec.p: It has been shown that Scheimpflug cameras might overestimate CCT. The increased reflectivity of the tear film in Scheimpflug imaging may explain greater corneal thickness to OCT [20]. Corneal thickness measurements may be influenced by tear film abnormalities, which were not present in the healthy eyes examined in our study [18]. Moreover, OCT systems have higher resolution and may allow more accurate detection of corneal edges than Scheimpflug-based imaging systems. Thus, they may capture more detailed changes in the corneal structure that are not visible with the Pentacam system, resulting in lower measurements [25]. Newer OCT systems with faster scan speeds can reduce artifacts caused by eye movements, which could influence CCT measurements [19]. For example, Scheimpflug-based imaging systems require up to 2 s per scan, while the RTVue-100 OCT imaging system requires only 0.31 s [22]. Different reference points for central measurements can also affect the measurements. Central measurements at the center may differ depending on whether the corneal vertex or the pupil center is used, and peripheral measurements may be averaged within different ranges or calculated from individual points depending on the system [21]. Differences in the time needed to scan the cornea and the intensity of stabilizing light can affect the stability of the patient’s vision and subsequent measurements.

Our study had several limitations that should be acknowledged. Firstly, the measurements were performed on a single eye per subject to avoid inter-eye correlation, which may have reduced variability and limited the generalizability of the results. Secondly, only healthy eyes were included, and thus the findings may not fully apply to eyes with corneal pathologies such as keratoconus or corneal dystrophies. Thirdly, patients with diabetes mellitus or clinically significant dry eye were not excluded, which may have influenced measurements due to tear film instability. Fourthly, ultrasonic pachymetry was not included for reference, preventing the absolute agreement between systems and the standard from being determined. Fifthly, although multiple comparisons were performed, no formal correction for multiple testing was applied, as the number of parameters was limited and p-values remained highly significant. Therefore, future studies including subjects with corneal disease and performing repeatability analyses are warranted to strengthen the clinical applicability of these findings.
In conclusion, CCT measurements were consistently higher with the Pentacam Scheimpflug-based imaging system than with the Revo FC OCT.
